analysis.one_liner: Requires uniform testing and public posting of health warnings at the nation's swimming beaches.
analysis.headline: The beach water safety bill was introduced in July 1996 with no cosponsors, referred to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to set national standards for how much harmful bacteria is allowed in ocean and Great Lakes waters where people swim, and required states to test those waters regularly and post warning signs when bacteria levels are unsafe. States that refused to adopt the standards would have them imposed federally, and federal grants would cover up to half the cost of testing. It was introduced in July 1996 and died without any action in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Swimmers, surfers, and beach visitors in coastal and Great Lakes states, who today face a patchwork of inconsistent state testing and often no warning when water is contaminated with bacteria from sewage overflows. Coastal tourism towns also stand to gain from reliable health information that protects both visitors and the industry's reputation.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to set national, science-based pathogen criteria for coastal and Great Lakes waters used for swimming, replacing a patchwork of inconsistent state testing methods [S2, S3].
Requires states to monitor beaches during public use and to post signs and notify local governments whenever water quality standards are violated, so swimmers know the risk [S2, S3].

Creates uniform procedures for detecting floatable debris and authorizes federal grants covering up to half of state implementation costs, plus funded research into better bacteria-detection methods [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: States and local governments would share the cost of routine water testing and signage (federal grants cover at most half). Facilities that discharge wastewater into coastal waters — sewage plants and industrial dischargers — would face compliance costs where their pollution triggers the new standards and closure warnings.
analysis.who_pays_short: States, local governments, and wastewater dischargers

drawbacks.text: States would bear at least half the cost of the new monitoring and standards programs, since federal grants are capped at 50 percent of implementation costs [S3].

States that did not adopt EPA-consistent standards within three years would have federal criteria imposed on them automatically, a preemption of state discretion that some would object to on federalism grounds [S2, S3].
The bill allowed the EPA Administrator to exempt discrete waters from monitoring requirements, a potential carve-out that could weaken protection in places judged less used [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — fewer waterborne illnesses, honest signage at the beach — are real and cheap relative to its cost: federal grants were capped at $4 million a year, with states covering the rest. The main burden falls on polluters and states, who would have to adopt uniform health standards instead of their own. An honest critic could note that a top-down federal mandate plus state matching costs is more than some states wanted, but the public-health payoff dwarfs the fiscal cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing, a vote, or cosponsors before Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 11, 1996 and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the same day [S1, S5].
On July 25, 1996 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where no further action was taken [S5].
The bill drew no cosponsors, and Congress adjourned on January 3, 1997 without any committee or floor vote [S4, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Municipal dischargers and coastal states were spared new testing and notification mandates; swimmers and beachgoers gained nothing. A substantially similar bill eventually passed as the BEACH Act of 2000, after Congress had ended.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and dischargers avoiding new mandates

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would mandate uniform beach water testing and public notification of contamination.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee / Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred to the subcommittee, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no positions beyond the sponsor's are on the record, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: Stricter standards mean more beach closures and advisory signs in the short run, which can hurt local tourism revenue, but reliable health information protects the long-term reputation of coastal recreation. The bill's own findings note coastal tourism generates billions annually [S3].

industries.industry: Municipal wastewater utilities and coastal polluters
industries.note: State standards based on EPA pathogen criteria would make sewage overflows and stormwater runoff a compliance problem, potentially requiring costly upgrades where discharges sicken swimmers [S2, S3].
The bill imposes federal testing, posting, and reporting requirements, but offsets them with federal grants covering up to half the implementation cost [S2, S3].
